source_user: A team wants lower serving cost through weight-only quantization. Define a fair comparison. Scenario variant 19: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: fix model and prompts; compare quality, memory, TTFT, TPOT, throughput, concurrency, kernel support, calibration set, and failure cases; report confidence intervals.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions and scope (variant 19): compare one model revision and tokenizer with identical prompts, decoding limits, request mix, hardware, topology, driver/runtime, serving build, batching policy, concurrency levels, power/thermal policy, and stopping rules. Change only weight precision. Record bit width, group size, scale/zero-point method, calibration corpus and outlier treatment; keep activation and KV-cache precision fixed unless a separate arm is declared. Because this is a system design review, first verify that the candidate kernel is actually selected and that any fallback path is counted; do not infer a cost benefit from parameter bytes alone. Use an authorized disposable benchmark, redact prompts and telemetry, and label every result measured, estimated, or unknown.

Hypothesis and decision rule: weight-only quantization reduces cost per successful output token while preserving predeclared quality, safety, functional correctness, and latency SLOs. Falsify it if paired held-out quality or safety scores breach their tolerance, correctness/error or retry rates regress, p95/p99 TTFT or TPOT breaches its SLO, throughput does not improve at matched concurrency, or the fully loaded cost per successful token fails to improve. Competing explanations are calibration-set mismatch, dequantization overhead, memory-bandwidth saturation, changed batching, thermal throttling, and kernel fallback.

Controlled experiment: build versioned full-precision and quantized artifacts from the same checkpoint. Use a preregistered, stratified calibration set for fitting only and a disjoint production-like held-out set for evaluation, plus adversarial and safety cases. Run randomized paired requests in alternating blocks at each fixed concurrency, with warm-up excluded, repeated across independent seeds/time windows and enough samples for bootstrap or appropriate confidence intervals. Measure quality and safety, exact-match/functional failures, memory high-water mark, TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, utilization, power, retries, timeouts, OOMs, kernel selection/fallback, and cleanup failures. Report medians and p95/p99 with 95% CIs, per workload slice, and cost as (hardware time, power, calibration, capacity, and operational overhead) divided by successful output tokens.

Confounders and safeguards: verify artifact hashes, deterministic config, thermal state, driver/kernel compatibility, prompt ordering, batching, and request arrival process; repeat across representative sequence lengths and inspect outliers. Do not pool failed requests into a misleading average. Start with a bounded canary and shadow or offline traffic; gate promotion on quality, safety, correctness, and tail-SLO thresholds. Route back to the versioned baseline, stop the canary, preserve minimal diagnostic logs with redaction/retention limits, and remove quantized artifacts and routing state only with authorization. Evidence is insufficient for production adoption if kernel fallback, held-out slices, sample size, uncertainty, or cost accounting is missing.

calibration or held-out distribution mismatch can conceal quality and safety regressions
thermal, batching, arrival-rate, or driver changes can confound paired comparisons
benchmark prompts and telemetry may contain sensitive data
rollback may leave quantized artifacts or routing state if cleanup is not verified
evidence_required: versioned checkpoint, tokenizer, quantization, calibration, kernel, runtime, and serving configurations with hashes

request-level latency, throughput, memory, utilization, power, error, retry, timeout, OOM, kernel/fallback, and cleanup traces across concurrency
